schools.summary: Gill reads the resumed 'parable' as deliberate — Job takes his discourse up again to give an account of his former life, that he might appear not the wicked man his friends made him.

Henry catches the mood before a word is spoken: 'Losers may have leave to speak,' and former prosperity is a man's most pleasing theme — yet Job wishes it back for God's glory and his reputation, not his ease.
Clarke lays out the plan of the whole speech: lament, former prosperity (vv.2-6), respect of young and nobles (vv.7-10), magistracy (vv.11-17), confidence and honour (vv.18-25).
Ellicott hears the wistfulness and warns with Solomon (Eccl. 7:10) against asking why the former days were better, though in Job's case the backward look was not without cause.

themes: the danger of preferring the past

schools.summary: Gill guards the wish from misreading — no carnal impatience, but a desire that the friends' reproach be lifted, his words again heeded, and himself able to do good; or merely to introduce the account of his former life.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'O that I had months like the times of yore' and settle the optative as 'O that I had'; Ellicott glosses 'preserved' as 'watched over me,' turning it into a question — 'when does God not watch over us, if we only knew it?'

Clarke reads the backward glance as an apology for his complaints, his prosperity not removed for any bad use of it; Wesley fixes 'preserved' against the present darkness — 'from all those miseries which now I feel.'

themes: O that I were as in months past
the days when God preserved me

schools.summary: Gill spreads the candle two ways — outward prosperity, 'the candle of the Lord,' shining like a torch on high or the meridian sun; or figuratively the light of grace, once shining clearly and now dimmed.

Clarke grounds the image in Eastern lamps pendant from the ceiling that shone on the guests' heads, and notes the nimbus given to great men; Wesley keeps 'darkness' plain — Job 'passed safely through many difficulties and dangers.'
Henry reads the candle as the light of God's countenance lifted on Job, by which he walked through darkness — the best of God's favours here but candle-light to what is reserved in the future state.

themes: his candle shined upon my head
walking through darkness by God's light

schools.summary: Gill takes 'the days of my youth' literally (feared God from youth), figuratively (his autumn, laden like a fruitful tree), or spiritually (the youth of his converted life); and 'the secret of God' as the secret assembly of devout worshippers.

Clarke presses the word to 'the days of my winter' (a root 'to strip bare'), reporting Harmer's rainy season and Good's 'summit/perfection'; takes 'secret of God' as the secret assembly of the devout, but reports Good's 'when God fortified my tent over me.'
Ellicott settles on 'my autumn,' the ripeness of Job's days (he now in winter), and renders 'the secret of God' as 'the counsel of God,' the lost intimate friendship.

sides.position: youth literally, or figuratively his autumn — the ripeness of prosperity
the days of his winter, from a root meaning to strip or make bare
his autumn, the ripeness and maturity of his days, against his present winter

debates.question: What is 'the secret of God upon my tabernacle'?

sides.position: the secret assembly of God — the devout worshippers gathered in Job's house
'when God fortified my tent over me' — a sheltering barrier (Good, as reported by Clarke)
the counsel of God, the intimate divine friendship

themes: the secret of God upon my tabernacle

schools.summary: Gill weighs the 'yet': not the providential presence God grants all men, but his special gracious presence, now withdrawn to Job's sense — the memory is also a prayer that God would return and show his face.

Henry makes the divine presence the crown of Job's comforts — 'God's presence, though it be but a cottage, makes it both a castle and a palace' — and counts the children about him among the family comforts, yet turns the loss to hope: having lost children, we have not lost our God.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'when the Almighty was still with me, my children round about me,' setting it as the centre of the backward look of vv.2-6.

themes: the Almighty was yet with me
God's presence makes a cottage a palace

schools.summary: Gill rejects a literal washing of palace steps as prodigality — the milk ran so freely Job stepped into it, an exaggeration like 'flowing with milk and honey'; or it means the washing of his feet, done here in dairy rather than water.
Henry reads the butter and oil as Job's own reckoning of wealth — not silver and gold for hoarding but butter and oil for use, for what is an estate good for unless we do good with it?
Clarke points back to his earlier note on the fatness of the land, letting butter and oil stand for the overflowing prosperity of Job's house.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'when my steps were bathed in cream, and the rock beside me poured forth streams of oil,' the oil pressed from olives among the rocks, so the barren stone seemed to run with plenty.

themes: the rock pouring rivers of oil

schools.summary: Gill notes Job did not indulge in ease at home but went abroad to care for the public welfare and administer justice at the gate, the seat of the courts, passing through the city in the pomp suited to his office.

Henry draws the moral: Job went out 'not in an affectation of pomp, but in an affection to justice,' judgment administered openly in the place of concourse where every man had free access and the guilty might hear and fear.

Clarke makes Job an emir, the supreme magistrate who 'prepared his seat in the street' and judged openly; Wesley marks that Job 'caused the seat of justice to be set,' plain proof he was a magistrate.
Ellicott notes that business was transacted at the gate, comparing the phrase 'the Sublime Porte' still used of the Turkish government.
Gill takes the young men's hiding as either veneration or fear, lest Job call them to account and reprove their youthful follies.

Keil and Delitzsch supply the custom — the young retired into the background, fearing his look of salutation, the aged stood and remained standing — illustrated from a Talmudic anecdote of the lesser not saluting the greater, which confirms Job's words.
Clarke: from all classes marked respect — the young shrank back through modesty, the aged rose from their seats, the elders who sat with the judge in legal causes.

Henry turns it to the fitness of each age — modesty becomes the young, majesty the aged; honour and fear due to magistrates (Rom. 13:7) — 'if a great and good man was thus reverenced, how is the great and good God to be feared!'

themes: the aged arose and stood up
how much more to fear God

schools.summary: Gill sees the princes break off their talk at Job's appearance, laying a restraint on their words till they had heard his opinion.
Clarke: they 'never ventured an opinion in opposition' to Job's, so persuaded were they of the justice of his decisions — men who would rather learn than be heard.
Henry gathers princes and nobles as men who paid Job deference for his extraordinary abilities; when he rose to speak they refrained talking to catch his meaning.

Keil and Delitzsch read the passage as the imposing impression of Job's presence, so that to hear of his prosperity was to call him happy; Ellicott compares the kings who shut their mouths at the exalted servant (Isa. 52:15).

Gill takes the nobles as a rank below the princes, but reports the guess that they were generals and army-leaders — 'sons of Mars,' bold and full of talk — the greater wonder that even these fell silent, their voice 'hid.'

Clarke parts the two Hebrew titles: princes as heads of townships, nobles as those privileged to stand before the chief ruler; reports too the reading that they were renowned speakers or eminent orators.
Henry draws the caution — happy the men with such gifts, but they must watch against pride; happy the people blessed with such men, a token for good to them.

sides.position: a noble rank below the princes — or perhaps military captains, 'sons of Mars'
court counsellors privileged to stand before the chief ruler, distinct from the township princes
renowned speakers or eminent orators (as others hold, reported by Clarke)

themes: the tongue cleaved to the mouth

schools.summary: Gill takes the ear of the common folk gathered to hear causes: they applauded Job's wisdom, wished him well, and accounted him blessed, not for his plenty only but for his grace and integrity as a magistrate.
Clarke reads this and the six following verses as a fine exhibition of unconfined philanthropy; Wesley glosses the eye's witness — it 'gave testimony to my pious, just, and blameless conversation.'
Henry finds what Job valued himself by — the unconstrained blessing of all about him — and presses the reciprocal duty of those helped to bless and pray for their benefactors.
Ellicott hears a direct negative to the charges of Eliphaz (Job 22:6), Job answering the slander not with argument but with the remembered blessing of the poor he was said to have wronged.

themes: the ear that blessed, the eye that witnessed

schools.summary: Gill marks that Job's honour was not for his riches but his goodness — when the poor cried he delivered them out of the hand of their oppressors.
Clarke hears a deliberate answer to Eliphaz, who charged Job with sending the widow away empty and breaking the arms of the fatherless (Job 22:9); Job appeals to facts, not argument.

Keil and Delitzsch reach past the deeds to the disposition — 'tsedeq,' a holding fast to God's will that calls for sympathizing love, its root (an Arabic word for what is hard, firm, straight, as a spear) making righteousness a rectitude that stands straight for the right, joined to 'mishpat.'
Henry values Job by his care for those least able to help themselves, who could neither merit his favour nor repay it — the poor had not only his ear but his hand.

Gill takes 'him ready to perish' as one on the edge of ruin through oppression, want, or false charges; Job searched his cause, respited and cleared him, and the rescued man's blessing 'came upon' Job and rested there.
Keil and Delitzsch fix the words — the 'interiturus' on the point of destruction, and the causative verb by which Job made the widow's heart sing aloud, compensating for the husband she had lost.

Henry keeps the pathos of both — the perishing saved, the sick tended, the falsely accused defended, and the widows sighing for grief made to sing for joy; a pleasure to a good man to give the grieving occasion to rejoice.

themes: the blessing of him ready to perish
the widow's heart made to sing

schools.summary: Gill insists the righteousness is not the imputed robe of the Redeemer (though Job had that by faith) but the legal righteousness of his office, worn constantly and covering him all over so no blemish showed.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'I put on justice, and it put me on'; Ellicott makes the interchange explicit — 'it clothed itself with me' — and hears in the reciprocity the Gospel truth of the interchange between Christ and the believer (cf. 'put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ,' Rom. 13:14).
Wesley: 'perhaps he did not wear these' literal ornaments, 'but his steady justice was to him instead of all those ornaments.'
Henry reads an habitual disposition to justice, put on as the girdle of his loins (Isa. 11:5); a magistrate doing his duty has therein an honour beyond gold or purple.

debates.question: Is the righteousness Job 'put on' his magisterial integrity only, or a shadow of imputed righteousness?

sides.position: the official, legal righteousness of his judgeship — expressly not imputed righteousness
the plain sense, but carrying the Gospel interchange of sin and righteousness between Christ and the believer

outliers.note: Reads the reciprocal 'it clothed itself with me' as the Gospel interchange — Christ bearing our sins while we are clothed with the robe of his righteousness.

themes: I put on righteousness and it clothed me

schools.summary: Gill spreads three senses — literal (guiding and providing for the bodily blind), civil (counselling the perplexed and oppressed), and spiritual (eyes to his blind heathen neighbours).
Clarke prefers the concrete picture of desert travel — Job furnished guides to those who did not know the way and set the worn-out forward on his camels.
Henry reads the civil sense and draws a rule: we best help others in the very thing wherein they are defective — and we may come to be blind or lame ourselves.
Keil and Delitzsch take it as the plain figure of a compassion supplying the bodily and spiritual wants of others.

debates.question: In what sense was Job 'eyes to the blind and feet to the lame'?

sides.position: literal — guiding and carrying the bodily blind and lame
civil — counselling and representing the legally helpless
and even spiritual — enlightening his blind heathen neighbours

schools.summary: Gill reads the fatherhood in a civil sense — the patron and advocate of the poor, who pleaded their cause, supplied their want, and gave them part of his own morsel.
Keil and Delitzsch hear a wordplay in the Hebrew — 'the carer for the care-full ones' — noting the fine ambiguity of the terms for father and needy.
Clarke fixes the judge's conscience: the cause he knew not he examined to the bottom, whatever the cost, that he might never pronounce a hasty judgment.
Henry expands the pains taken — Job heard both sides impartially and never judged a man righteous merely for being first to plead his own cause (Prov. 18:17).

themes: the cause I knew not I searched out

schools.summary: Clarke unfolds the hunting metaphor — a beast of prey carries off a sheep, the huntsman breaks his jaws and delivers the spoil, as David rescued the lamb from the lion (1 Sam. 17:34).
Henry marks the precision: Job broke not their necks but their jaws — took away their power of mischief and plucked the spoil from between their teeth; a judge needs the courage of a commander.

Gill takes the broken grinders of the beast of prey, and gives the figure a double edge — Job disabled tyrants, but also confuted the arguments the wicked made against the poor, exposing their weakness.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'broke the teeth of the wicked, and cast the spoil forth out of his teeth' as the climax of Job's championship of the helpless.

debates.question: How far does breaking 'the jaws of the wicked' reach?

sides.position: the shattering of the oppressor's power to harm — the beast robbed of its prey
that, and also the confuting of the wicked's arguments and pleas

themes: breaking the jaws of the wicked
plucking the spoil from the teeth

schools.summary: Gill reads the 'nest' tenderly — Job thought death far off, and that he would die at home with his children about him, the opposite of his present stripped and childless state.

Henry hears a man in a warm nest who hoped nothing would remove him till death did; a confidence good if from faith in God's promise, ill-grounded if from conceit of our own wisdom, like the rich fool's 'take thine ease.'

Keil and Delitzsch prefer 'like the phoenix' over 'as the sand,' the deathless bird chiming with the 'nest'; Ellicott finds the hope touchingly unconscious and reports the proposal to transpose vv.18-20 to the chapter's end (cf. the close of ch. 31).
Clarke: having lived soberly, Job concluded he would live long and his posterity multiply as the sands; Wesley draws the note — 'see how apt even good men are to set death at a distance.'

debates.question: Does Job hope to multiply his days 'as the sand,' or 'like the phoenix'?

sides.position: as the sand — days countless as the grains of sand (the old versions and many moderns)
holders: the old versions (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

sides.position: like the phoenix — a life renewed from its own ashes, chiming with the 'nest'

debates.question: Should vv.18-20 be transposed to the end of the chapter?

sides.position: some would transpose them, their natural place in one sense
yet in another sense less natural, better left where they stand

themes: I shall die in my nest
multiply my days as the sand

schools.summary: Gill lays out the tenses — past (the ground of Job's confidence), present ('my root is spread out'), or future (a hope it would ever so continue, as some Jewish and Christian interpreters render) — all true of Job in their way.

Ellicott comes down for the present, 'my root is spread out, and the dew lieth'; Keil and Delitzsch take the spread root and night-long dew as a life fed from earth and heaven both, a borrowed flourishing owing nothing to the tree itself.
Clarke reads a healthy tree by a rivulet, flourishing in all seasons, its leaf never withering (cf. Ps. 1:3; Jer. 17:8).

debates.question: In what tense is the well-watered-tree to be read?

sides.position: past — the ground of a confidence Job felt
present — a prosperity still felt unshaken
future — a hope that it would ever so continue

themes: the root spread by the waters
a tree that could not wither

schools.summary: Gill, in the briefest note, keeps the tense alive — the glory 'was,' or 'is,' or 'shall be.'

Clarke gives the freshness a vegetative sense — blossom and mellow fruit always in season, the bow renewed meaning means never lacking; Wesley parts the clauses — 'glory' the growing reputation, 'bow' the strength (bow the chief weapon of war, Gen. 49:24; 1 Sam. 2:4).
Keil and Delitzsch render 'mine honour will remain ever fresh, and my bow will become young in my hand' — honour undimmed and strength renewing its youth.

Henry: God's favour continuing, Job's glory stayed fresh, for only constant goodness keeps a man's glory from withering; his renewed bow the emblem of a strength he thought inexhaustible, fearing neither Sabean nor Chaldean.

themes: the bow renewed in the hand

schools.summary: Gill paints universal attention — men all ear to Job, high and low, rich and poor alike — and Job concluded they always would.
Clarke refers the reader back, the same idea as the silence and blessing of vv.9-11, resumed to fill out the picture of Job's former sway.
Keil and Delitzsch fix the posture — 'hearkened and waited,' silent at his decision — and note the pausal form of 'and waited,' a mark of the poet's care.
Henry names Job the oracle of his country, consulted and acquiesced in as one; the wrangling parties agreed at least to refer the matter to Job and abide his decision.
Gill reads unqualified agreement — after Job spoke, men made no reply, altered nothing, contradicted nothing; they 'differed not,' but rested in what he said as full to the purpose.
Clarke: Job's speech 'dropped upon them' as refreshing dew, encouraging and strengthening; Wesley: it dropped 'as the rain that comes gently upon the earth, most acceptable and beneficial.'
Keil and Delitzsch take the 'dropping' as the distilling of Job's speech, a slow soaking descent, not a torrent but a nourishing fall.
Henry joins the two — none meddled with a subject exhausted, and his speech dropped as welcome rain, waited for as the parched ground waits for showers.

themes: after my words they spake not again

schools.summary: Gill takes the former rain, falling in autumn after seedtime; as the husbandman waited daily for it, so the people waited for Job's coming into their assemblies.
Clarke explains both rains — the latter falling before harvest to fill the grain, the former about seedtime to swell the seed — the opened mouth a metaphor from ground chapped with drought.
Henry draws the likeness — the wise drink in wise discourse as the earth drinks the rain that comes often upon it (Heb. 6:7).
Keil and Delitzsch take the opened mouth as the gesture of thirst, the hearers gaping for Job's words as the cracked field gapes for the spring rains.

Gill reads the laughter as Job's rare familiarity, too grave a man for them to think he jested; or, by another rendering, 'they would not be bold' — his familiarity bred no contempt, but kept their awe.

Clarke reads the incredulity of joy — his smile 'news too good to be true' (cf. those who 'believed not for joy,' Luke 24:41) — and the undimmed light of his countenance as a benevolence they gave no occasion to withdraw; Wesley: they could scarce believe their eyes, and were careful to give no occasion to change his countenance.
Ellicott inclines to the joy-reading: they would not believe Job could be so affable, but looked up to him with the greatest deference.
Henry holds affection and awe together — those Job smiled on could scarce believe it for joy, yet he so dispensed his favours that his freedom never made his smiles cheap.

debates.question: What does 'they believed it not' mean?

sides.position: they could scarcely credit his rare smile for very joy — news too good to be true
'they would not be bold' — his familiarity never tempted them to presume

themes: if I laughed on them they believed it not

schools.summary: Gill reads the counsellor — Job marked out their way in civil matters and instructed them in their duty in religious ones, they preferring his judgment to their own.

Clarke finds Job's whole public and private life at once — supreme magistrate, captain-general dwelling as a king among his troops, and a man not above the meanest office of kindness, comforting the mourners ('Noble Job!'); Wesley parts the titles — prince, king whose presence puts courage into an army, and welcome comforter.

Henry makes Job the sovereign of his country, uniting a commander's authority with a comforter's tenderness (felt now that he is himself a mourner), and a type of Christ on whom the blessing of a perishing world comes (Ps. 72:2).
Ellicott closes on the pathos — Job the type of suffering humanity, of man waiting for redemption but as yet unredeemed, who in that character points on to Christ the Redeemer.

themes: Job as a type of Christ
